video_title: Why You Can't Drive Anywhere In This Part of Alaska
transcript: Juno, Alaska is one of the strangest major cities located anywhere on the North American continent. At least from a transportation and logistics perspective. With just over 31,000 residents, Juno is one of Alaska's top three largest cities. But it's still dramatically smaller than Anchorage is. The Greater Anchorage metropolitan region is home to roughly 400,000 people, more than half of Alaska's entire population and around 13 times as many people as live in Juno. As you would expect, Anchorage is also Alaska's largest economic center and represents roughly half of the entire statewide GDP all on its own. And yet, despite all of that, Juno is actually the Alaska state capital, where Alaska's legislature meets and where many of the most important government offices are located. But that's not really what makes this whole situation so unusual. Far more bizarre is the fact that Juno is also just an extremely difficult place for most of the state's own population to actually reach at all. You see, Juno is located approximately 573 mi away from Anchorage as the crow flies. But there are absolutely zero roads that actually connect the two cities together. In fact, there aren't even any roads connecting Juno to anywhere else in the outside world of North America either. The only practical ways to travel between Anchorage and Juno are to either fly or to combine an agonizingly long road trip through Canada with a long ferry journey baked in. A direct flight between the two cities only takes a little less than 2 hours. But taking your own car between them requires driving for roughly 750 m through Alaska and Canada's Yukon Territory to the small town of Hannes [music] back in Alaska where you have to load your car up onto a ferry for another 4 and 1/2 hour maritime journey the rest of the way to Juno with an additional 2 hours that's generally required beforehand for vehicle check-in. Altogether, the road trip between Anchorage and Juno usually takes as much as 25 hours to complete, assuming that the ferry is functioning and isn't delayed by inclement weather or maintenance. This would be akin to living in Dallas, Texas, and having to drive all the way out to San Francisco just to visit your own state capital. And of course, if you miss the ferry, it could all take substantially longer. The reason why becomes more obvious when you look at Juno's local geography. The city is wedged along a narrow strip of coastline between the Castano Channel and the sprawling landscape of glaciers and mountains extending all the way across the international border into British Columbia. It's a very, very hard place to actually get to or out of by land. Juno has plenty of local roads connecting its own downtown neighborhoods and airport, but none of these roads lead anywhere outside of the local area. They all just come to an abrupt end at the water, the mountains, or in the surrounding wilderness. And because Juno is physically located on the North American mainland itself rather than on an island, this gives it a particularly unique distinction. Juno is the largest city on the North American continent today in the 21st century that isn't connected to anywhere else on the continent by road, making it effectively function like an island from a transportation and logistics perspective. It's the only American state capital outside of Hawaii that cannot be accessed directly by land. And by extension, it's arguably the most isolated city of more than 30,000 people anywhere on the North American continent today as well. And perhaps most remarkably of all, Juno is also far from the only place in this part of Alaska with this same problem. Juno lies within a greater region that's known as Southeast Alaska or sometimes the Alaskan panhandle. a region stretching for roughly 500 miles along the Pacific coast between British Columbia and the ocean. The region is large, covering an area that's slightly larger than the US state of Maine that is home to approximately 70,000 full-time residents. Nearly one in every 10 Alaskans. And yet almost the entirety of the panhandle is completely disconnected from the rest of the continental highway system. Only three principal communities within the panhandle. Hannes, Skagway, and the tiny settlement of Haidider actually have any road connections to anywhere else in the outside world. And even all of those connections lead through Canada rather than directly through Alaska. For virtually everybody else who lives here in places like Juno, Ketchacan, Sitka, Petersburg, and Wrangle, there simply aren't any highways for them leading out of their own region. And on top of that, most of these panhandle communities aren't even connected to each other by roads either. Juno, Ketchacan, and Sitka, the panhandle's top three largest population centers, all possess their own independent road systems that don't connect with each other or anywhere else. Traveling between any of them requires taking a plane or loading up your vehicle onto a ferry, just like leaving the region for anywhere else in the rest of the continent does, too. So, why did this bizarre logistical situation exist here? Why hasn't the US built up a highway network that connects Southeast Alaska and its 70,000 residents to the outside world yet? And why was the state capital ever placed here in such an inaccessible location in the first place? To begin with understanding all of that, we need to go back to Alaska's early settlement history. Because while Anchorage is overwhelmingly the largest population center in the state today, that wasn't always the case. And it's actually kind of a more recent phenomenon. When Russian fur traders began establishing outposts and settlements in colonial Alaska during the late 18th century, they concentrated largely on the coast, which of course was a lot easier for them to reach by ship than the remote interior was. Southeast Alaska was especially appealing to these early trappers and settlers because of its comparatively much more mild maritime climate. While much of Alaska, especially the interior, experiences savagely cold [music] winters, the panhandle region is more moderated by the influence of the Pacific Ocean, giving it a climate that more resembles that of Washington State or British Columbia than the rest of Alaska. Its proximity to valuable sea otter hunting grounds was also economically important to the early Russians, as well as its proximity to the coast of California for trade further to the south. For these broader reasons, the Russians eventually established their colonial capital in Alaska at modern-day Sitka in the early 19th century. And since virtually all long-d distanceance transportation in Russian Alaska took place by ship along the coast, there was very little reason for them to ever build any roads into the interior. When the US later purchased Alaska from the Russians in 1867, the Americans simply continued retaining Sitka as the administrative center, at least at first. But then a bit over a decade later in 1880, gold was discovered near present-day Juno. And the resulting rush of miners and prospectors in search of their fortune rapidly transformed the Gastino Channel into one of Alaska's most important economic regions. Huge gold mines developed around Juno that surged the region's local population. While the even larger Klondike gold rush that began just to the north in the Yukon Territory in 1896 brought tens of thousands of additional prospectors through southeast Alaska's ports on their way, which of course increased Juno's population even further. Juno rapidly surpassed Sitka in both population and economic importance as a result. And by 1906, the capital was formally relocated to Juno in order to reflect this. And at that time, Juno's location actually made a considerable amount of sense. Southeast Alaska was closer to the lower 48 than most of the rest of the territory was. Its comparatively milder climate allowed maritime shipping throughout the year, while its ports provided access to the other major settlements that were scattered along the coast, too. So, after Alaska became a state in 1959, residents repeatedly began debating about whether the capital should be moved again, like it was from Sitka to Chunau back in the 19th century. And interestingly, Alaska has voted on more capital relocation related ballot measures than any other state in the union has by far with no less than nine such measures appearing before Alaskan voters over the past several decades. Proposals in 1960 and 1962 were simply rejected. But then in 1974, something rather extraordinary happened. Voters in the state actually approved relocating the capital away from Juno with 56.6% supporting the move. Alaskan voters selected the small town of Willow as the proposed location for their new capital. And so in what has sometimes been described as being in typical Alaskan fashion, voters approved the ballot to move the capital, but then later rejected the ballot that would have actually funded it.
